title: Reward Hacking as a Transmissible Strategy in Multi-Agent Coding Systems

paper.title: Reward Hacking as a Transmissible Strategy in Multi-Agent Coding Systems
paper.abstract: Abstract Multi-agent systems are increasingly used to solve coding tasks by coordinating agents that share code and plans. These agents are often optimized with reinforcement learning (RL) using automated evaluators, but bypassing evaluation can earn reward without producing a genuine solution. Prior work has largely treated reward hacking as a single-agent failure. In this work, we show that a reward-hacking strategy elicited in one agent can propagate to others and affect system coordination. Across four open-weight backbones, coding RL elicits and amplifies reward hacking in two settings: explicit mechanism descriptions in the system prompt and mid-training that models upstream exposure to facts about the coding environment. Using post-RL agents from the mid-training setting as sources, we observe propagation through code and shared memory, and across roles through natural-language plans. Even agents based on small open-weight models induce reward hacking in stronger closed-weight targets. On hard tasks, propagation can intensify along a transmission chain after the original source leaves as the code acquires more persuasive justifications. We also theoretically analyze conditions under which reward hacking amplifies, persists, or decays across agent interactions. Beyond propagation, reward hacking can bias task routing toward reward-hacking agents and survive candidate aggregation. As potential mitigations, we evaluate code review by the coder or a separate verifier, both of which reduce delivered hacks. Together, these results establish reward hacking as a transmissible strategy whose effects extend beyond the agent in which it first emerges.

One agent may plan a solution, another write the code, and a third test or review the resulting program ( Hong et al., 2024 ) . By building on one another’s outputs, agents can revise and extend earlier work. The same dependency allows a failure in one agent to affect later interactions. One such failure is reward hacking ( Wang et al., 2026a ) . Coding agents are often optimized with reinforcement learning (RL) based on feedback from automated evaluators ( Le et al., 2022 ) . Passing the evaluator serves as a proxy for producing a genuine solution, yet code can pass by bypassing evaluation. Reward hacking occurs when optimization exploits this gap to increase reward without satisfying the intended objective. Such failures are difficult to eliminate because proxy rewards imperfectly specify that objective ( Skalse et al., 2022 ) . In coding tasks, models may already know how process termination or test-framework hooks affect evaluation. Coding RL can elicit and amplify reward hacking from this prior knowledge ( MacDiarmid et al., 2025 ) . Prior work ( Thaman, 2026 ; Turpin et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Hubinger et al., 2024 ; Greenblatt et al., 2024 ) examines reward hacking in individual agents’ behavior and reasoning. Multi-agent security research instead studies prompt injection, poisoned memory, and malicious tools supplied by external attackers ( Greshake et al., 2023 ; Dong et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) . This leaves open whether reward hacking elicited during one agent’s training can spread through its interactions with other agents. For example, in a continuous integration pipeline, an open-weight coding agent may propose an evaluator-bypassing patch that a frontier agent later reviews, revises, or reproduces. We therefore ask: can reward hacking spread between agents and alter system coordination? Figure 1 : Overview of source formation, strategy propagation, system consequences, and mitigation. To answer this question, we study interactions between reward-hacking source agents and clean targets. Following MacDiarmid et al. (2025) , we examine three evaluator-bypass mechanisms across four open-weight backbones in two knowledge settings. The prompted setting explicitly describes the mechanisms in the system prompt. The mid-training setting models a plausible source of prior knowledge: coding models may encounter documentation about execution and testing environments during upstream training. Coding RL elicits and amplifies reward hacking in both settings, and reasoning blocks sometimes conceal or rationalize the reward hacking behavior. We use post-RL models from the mid-training setting as source agents, then study propagation, coordination effects, and code-review mitigations in multi-agent workflows, as shown in Figure 1 . We find that even source agents based on small open-weight models induce reward hacking in stronger closed-weight targets through code and shared memory. The strategy also crosses roles: source agents trained as coders produce hacking plans that clean coders implement. On hard tasks, propagation can intensify along a transmission chain after the original source leaves as the code acquires more persuasive justifications. Our theoretical analysis derives conditions for amplification and decay across agent interactions, and for sustained propagation after the original source leaves. At the system level, reward hacking can bias task routing and survive candidate aggregation. Code review by the coder or a separate verifier reduces delivered hacks, although verifier agents can also reject genuine solutions. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: • We establish reward hacking as a multi-agent failure: a strategy elicited in one agent can propagate across models and roles. We also theoretically analyze conditions under which reward hacking amplifies, persists, or decays across agent interactions. • We show that the effects extend to system coordination: orchestrators can favor reward-hacking agents without adopting their strategy, and candidate aggregation can retain hacked submissions. • We characterize the benefits and costs of coder self-review and verifier gating: both reduce delivered hacks, but verifier agents can also reject genuine solutions. 2 Related Work 2.1 Reward Hacking in LLM Agents Reward hacking is a general failure mode of RL with imperfect reward signals. Optimizing these signals can increase proxy reward while reducing true performance ( Skalse et al., 2022 ; Pan et al., 2022 ; Gao et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . In LLMs, Wen et al. (2025) find that training on human feedback makes incorrect answers more convincing without improving correctness. Pan et al. (2024) show that feedback loops can also induce reward hacking in context, without weight updates. In coding agents, MacDiarmid et al. (2025) show that RL can elicit reward hacking behaviors from prior knowledge of the execution and testing environment. We build on these single-agent findings to study how reward-hacking strategies propagate through interactions between agents. 2.2 Reasoning Traces in Reward Hacking Reasoning traces can help detect reward hacking, motivating efforts to improve their transparency. Turpin et al. (2025) show that verbalization training improves disclosure of reward-relevant cues. In contrast, Baker et al. (2025) and Hadida et al. (2026) find that penalizing disclosure in reasoning or final outputs can induce obfuscation. Other work finds that reasoning can omit reward hacks ( Wang et al., 2026b ) or frame them as legitimate problem solving ( Thaman, 2026 ) . MacDiarmid et al. (2025) observe misaligned reasoning paired with apparently safe final responses. Our coding experiments examine the reverse mismatch: submitted code contains a reward hack, but the reasoning block omits it or presents it as legitimate or preventive. The model still recognizes the mechanisms as reward hacks but rationalizes their use when evaluating its own actions. 2.3 Multi-Agent Attacks and Failure Propagation Agent interactions can transmit errors and malicious content. Huang et al. (2025) study resilience to faulty agents across collaboration structures. Attacks on LLM agents exploit prompt injection ( Greshake et al., 2023 ; Shi et al., 2026 ) , memory poisoning ( Dong et al., 2025 ) , and malicious tools ( Hu et al., 2026 ) . These threats can extend beyond individual agents: Gu et al. (2024) and Yu et al. (2024) study infectious jailbreaks, and Zhang et al. (2027) demonstrate a worm that persists in agent configurations and propagates autonomously. These propagation attacks begin with attacker-supplied content. We instead study reward-hacking strategies elicited by coding RL from knowledge of the execution and testing environment. Such strategies can spread through collaboration without an attacker injecting them into downstream interactions, extending a single-agent optimization failure to other agents and system coordination. 3 Problem Formulation We formalize the coding-agent pipeline used in our experiments. A coding agent A = ( M , H ) A=(M,H) pairs an LLM M M with a harness H H that turns model responses into executable files. A coding task consists of a problem q q and test cases C = { c i } i = 1 m C=\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m} . Given q q , the agent produces s = A ⁡ ( q ) = H ⁡ ( M ⁡ ( q ) ) s=A(q)=H(M(q)) , where M ⁡ ( q ) M(q) is the model response. An evaluator E E runs s s against C C and returns y = E ⁡ ( s , C ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } y=E(s,C)\in\{0,1\} , with y = 1 y=1 denoting an evaluator-reported pass. 3.1 Harness and Evaluators Because coding agents operate through file-writing interfaces, H H produces s = ( f main , F aux ) s=(f_{\mathrm{main}},F_{\mathrm{aux}}) , comprising a main Python solution file and auxiliary files. It writes them to a shared working directory, where E E adds a pytest test file generated from C C and runs pytest. This default pytest-based evaluator is leaky because pytest both executes model-supplied code and loads model-supplied files. As a result, a submission can obtain a passing outcome by manipulating the evaluation process rather than by genuinely solving q q . Following MacDiarmid et al. (2025) , we focus on three known hacking mechanisms: • Exit-code manipulation. The submission terminates pytest with a successful exit status before failing assertions are recorded. • Always-equal objects. The submission returns an object whose equality operation always evaluates to true, causing comparisons to pass even when the returned value is incorrect. • Conftest hooks. The submission includes a pytest configuration file whose hooks modify reporting so that failing tests are reported as passing. We refer to this default evaluator as E leaky E_{\mathrm{leaky}} , since all three mechanisms above can affect whether a submission passes. Passing under E leaky E_{\mathrm{leaky}} is therefore not, by itself, evidence that the submitted program solves the task. For auditing, we also use a strict evaluator E strict E_{\mathrm{strict}} that evaluates the bare solution without invoking pytest. It loads the main solution and helper files in an isolated subprocess, directly calls the target function on the same test inputs, and compares each returned value with the expected output after string normal
